title: What Happens Next? Anticipating Future Motion by Generating Point Trajectories
claim: State-of-the-art generators fail at physically plausible motion, showing distortion, splitting, vanishing and spontaneous appearance of objects over time.
layout: 1 row of 5 frames, left-to-right, colored boxes mark failures
description: A single horizontal strip of five rendered video frames from a generated video of a simulated scene with colored 3D objects (orange cubes, purple cylinders and spheres, a green sphere and cube) on a gray floor. The leftmost frame is labeled 'Input'. The next frames are labeled 'Next frame', 'Middle of the video' (two frames) and 'Last frame'. A long arrow labeled 'Time' runs beneath the frames from the second frame to the right edge. Colored bounding boxes (magenta, cyan, blue, purple) outline individual objects across frames and highlight failures: objects change shape, split into several parts, disappear, or appear from nowhere. The eye is drawn first to the bold 'Input' label and then along the boxes through time.
caption: State-of-the-art video generators frequently produce unrealistic motion. Even state-of-the-art models, such as WAN 14B shown here, often struggle to produce accurate, realistic and coherent motion. Common failure modes include \ulcool{cool0}{distorted object geometry}, \ulcool{cool9}{objects splitting into multiple parts}, \ulcool{cool4}{objects disappearing}, and \ulcool{cool6}{objects spontaneously appearing} throughout the video.
abstract: We consider the problem of forecasting motion from a single image, i.e., predicting how objects in the world are likely to move, without the ability to observe other parameters such as the object velocities or the forces applied to them. We formulate this task as conditional generation of dense trajectory grids with a model that closely follows the architecture of modern video generators but outputs motion trajectories instead of pixels. This approach captures scene-wide dynamics and uncertainty, yielding more accurate and diverse predictions than prior regressors and generators. We extensively evaluate our method on simulated data, demonstrate its effectiveness on downstream applications such as robotics, and show promising accuracy on real-world intuitive physics datasets. Although recent state-of-the-art video generators are often regarded as world models, we show that they struggle with forecasting motion from a single image, even in simple physical scenarios such as falling blocks or mechanical object interactions, despite fine-tuning on such data. We show that this limitation arises from the overhead of generating pixels rather than directly modeling motion.
